description: I'm a student passionate about game development, coding, software, web development, design, art and animation. I'm fascinated by space exploration, especially the Moon and Mars. I'd love to build an interactive, engaging space-themed game that makes science fun. I'm looking for creative teammates skilled in programming, game/web development, UI/UX, animation, 3D modelling, and scientific research. Enthusiasm and teamwork matter more than experience. Let's build something out of this world! 🚀
summary:
**Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer** is an educational simulation game that puts players in charge of a Mars outpost for a 50-day mission. Players explore seven connected habitat rooms, work with a crew of five astronauts, solve science-based puzzles, respond to unexpected events, and manage essential resources such as oxygen, water, food, power, and crew health.

The project addresses the challenge of preparing students for future lunar and Martian exploration by turning complex space-science concepts into interactive, decision-based learning experiences. Players discover how life-support systems, food production, energy management, radiation safety, and teamwork are interconnected. Daily mission reports reinforce what they learn, while different endings reflect the consequences of their decisions.

Inspired by NASA and Canadian Space Agency educational resources, the game also features a NASA Astronomy Picture of the Day gallery. It is important because it makes space science more accessible and engaging for young learners, encouraging scientific curiosity, critical thinking, problem-solving, and an understanding of the challenges of living beyond Earth.
details:
Project Details — Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive educational simulation game in which players take command of a Mars outpost for a 50-day mission. The player explores seven connected habitat rooms and manages a crew of five astronauts, each with a specialised role.

Throughout the mission, players complete daily objectives, interact with habitat equipment, solve science-based puzzles, assign crew members to tasks and respond to unexpected events. They must balance essential resources such as oxygen, water, food and power while monitoring temperature, radiation indicators, crew health and morale.

At the end of each mission day, an automatic report summarises completed tasks, resource changes and a scientific concept or takeaway. The mission concludes with different endings based on the player's decisions and the condition of the habitat.

2. What are its benefits?

The game makes complex space-science concepts easier to understand through interaction rather than passive reading. It encourages students to think critically, solve problems, manage limited resources and understand how different systems in a space habitat depend on one another.

It also introduces younger learners to topics such as life-support systems, sustainable food production, radiation safety, energy management and astronaut health in an engaging environment.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to make space science more accessible and interesting to young students, especially those who may not have access to advanced science-learning facilities.

By placing players in realistic-inspired mission scenarios, we want to encourage curiosity about space exploration and help them understand the scientific thinking, teamwork and planning required for future lunar and Martian missions.

4. What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed as a browser-based game using:

  • HTML — game structure and interface.
  • CSS — visual design, layouts and animations.
  • JavaScript — gameplay logic, resource simulation, puzzles, crew behaviour, mission progression and interactions.
  • HTML Canvas 2D — habitat rendering, characters, equipment and movement.
  • Node.js — local server and secure NASA API proxy.
  • NASA APOD API — recent astronomy images, descriptions and educational content in the in-game Deep Space Gallery.
  • Local Storage — saving mission progress and player preferences.

AI-assisted coding tools were used to support development and debugging. The game does not require an external AI model to run its core gameplay.

5. How is the project creative?

Instead of presenting space science as a collection of facts, we turned it into a mission where every decision has consequences. Players do not simply read about oxygen recycling or food production; they interact with the systems responsible for keeping their habitat operational.

The combination of habitat exploration, specialised crew assignments, resource management, interactive puzzles, unexpected events and automatic daily learning reports creates a connected learning experience.

A scripted assistant named P.I.X.E.L. acts as a mission guide, helping players understand objectives and important system warnings. The NASA Deep Space Gallery also connects the game to real astronomy discoveries and images.

6. What factors did our team consider?

We considered the intended age group, educational value, scientific relevance, accessibility and technical feasibility.

The game was designed to be understandable for younger students without removing the complexity of the decisions involved. We used simplified resource values and outcomes for gameplay, while avoiding presenting them as actual Mars measurements or scientific forecasts.

We also considered offline usability, local save functionality, a lightweight browser-based design and the limitations of building a working simulation within the hackathon timeframe.

Our intention was to create more than a space-themed game: we wanted to build an interactive introduction to the challenges of sustaining human life beyond Earth.
